extracted.intended_audience: qualitative health researchers, postgraduate students, and practitioners interested in using media and text-based sources as naturally occurring data
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, appraising, and analysing traditional media (TV, radio, film, newspapers, magazines, advertising) and text-based sources (policy documents, medical records, notes) as naturally occurring data in qualitative health research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat media and text-based sources as naturally occurring primary data
rubrics_metrics.description: Media sources (television, documentaries, newspapers, magazines) and text-based materials (policy documents, medical notes, police/court transcripts, social care reports, natural diaries) can be considered primary, naturally occurring data rather than only secondary sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often positioned as secondary in textbooks, but the chapter argues they can be primary data for qualitative research. Use recordings and original texts as data for analysis; recognise these materials are produced in-context and thus are 'naturally occurring'. Examples: TV documentaries, hospital medical notes, policy documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand media's dual role: reporting (factual) vs representing (fictional/constructed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between media that report factual science-based health issues and media that represent health through fictional or dramatized content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should attend to both factual accuracy and the meanings produced by representations. Example: news reports vs fictional television characters; film/drama can shape public meanings (e.g., 'Rain Man' and autism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess accuracy versus sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how media coverage compares to scientific findings and identify instances of sensationalising or exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should check accuracies and note sensationalist framing. Be aware that exaggeration can originate in academic press releases (Sumner et al., 2014). Tasks include comparing media claims with scientific evidence and documenting misrepresentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse agenda-setting and selection effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate which health issues receive media attention and why, and how this selection shapes public perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider media's agenda-setting function (which diseases/issues are 'newsworthy'), and how selection contributes to public construction of risk and concern. Use comparative analyses across outlets/countries to explore differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine source use and journalistic practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate who journalists rely on (e.g., medical staff, specialist reporters) and how source selection and reporter expertise influence coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for use of trusted sources, specialist reporters' technical knowledge, and organisational power dynamics. Assess how these practices affect neutrality, balance, and accuracy (Leask et al., 2010).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider production purpose, editorial decisions and framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the producers' aims, editing, and the intended purpose of media items when using them as data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentaries, chat shows, news, and adverts are edited/purposive. Example guidance: 'think about what the documentary was produced for, how it was produced, and the fact that it will have been edited for a certain purpose.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose media type to fit research question (medium affordances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select TV, radio, documentaries, films, news, chat shows, advertisements, newspapers, magazines, policy documents or medical notes based on their specific analytical affordances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television/radio give audio-visual and interactional data; newspapers/magazines provide accessible textual/visual corpora; policy documents and medical records offer institutional and procedural detail. Match medium to analytic aims (e.g., representation studies, interactional analysis, policy implementation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quantitative and/or qualitative analytic techniques appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Media data can be analysed with either quantitative or qualitative methods (or both); choose methods that answer the research question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Daykin et al.'s mixed quantitative/qualitative analysis of radio output; content analysis of policy documents; discourse or conversation analysis for interactional data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for cultural and contextual scope and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that media reach is international but analyses cannot fully account for all cultural contexts; be cautious in generalisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare media across countries where relevant (e.g., mental health coverage differs UK vs USA/Australia). Be explicit about cultural limits of the dataset.

rubrics_metrics.name: For television and radio: analyse both reporting and representation dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat television and radio as sources for both how they report health issues and how they represent health through narratives and characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine news, documentaries, chat shows, radio calls, and fictional programmes for both factual content and representational frames (e.g., stigma, normalisation). Radio call-ins provide insight into lay claims and presenter influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage live/in-situ news interviews for immediate emotional data (with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: News interviews (studio or on-the-scene) capture real-time reactions and emotions that can be analysed as raw naturally occurring data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to study emotional expressions and interactional dynamics, but remember news selection is not neutral and interviews are influenced by journalistic agendas and institutional constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat chat shows as entertainment-framed sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise chat shows are designed as light entertainment and may present items as factual while serving entertainment purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing chat shows, account for guest selection, the show's purpose, and performative aspects of hosts/guests. Examples include phone-ins, 'agony aunt' segments, debates on controversial issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentaries: interrogate claims of objectivity and examine multiple accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Although documentaries present as factual, they are editorial constructs; analyse how they construct reality and whose voices they include (experts, lay people).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use documentaries to track social/cultural/historical trends and to compare accounts from different actors. Note editorial selection and the role of lay participants in normalising medical perspectives (Hodgetts & Chamberlain, 1999).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse advertising for rhetorical/persuasive strategies and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat advertisements as data to examine persuasive techniques, stereotyping, target audiences, and the significance of placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider controversial content used to provoke conversation, placement (which programme/time), stereotyping implications, and marketing/branding roles (e.g., food ads targeting children).

rubrics_metrics.name: For newspapers and magazines: use accessibility but account for political alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers and magazines are readily available and cost-effective data sources, but their political affiliations and editorial slants shape content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these sources for comparative analyses (local/national/international), historical studies, and to analyse visual-text relationships in magazines; be mindful of political positioning when interpreting findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use visual material in magazines/film as analytic data
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse images and visual accompaniments as integral to meaning production, not just textual content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: compare visual images of women over time; examine adverts' visuals for stereotyping; consider film imagery and memorable representations shaping discourse (Garner et al., 2016).

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy document analysis: examine original conceptualisation, intended outcomes, and implementation alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy documents can reveal how policies were framed, intended outcomes, funding priorities, and help assess alignment between statements and implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse not just documents but also implementation (e.g., staff responses, practice). Predefined criteria and document maps are useful tools to measure alignment (Cheung et al., 2010). Remember policy writers may not fully articulate intended outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use medical records/notes with heightened ethical safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical records/notes are rich but highly sensitive naturally occurring data requiring careful ethical consideration and access procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether documents require special permissions, anonymisation, and different analytic approaches. Medical notes may be primary or contextual data; consider institutional relevance and whether analytic methods differ from other source types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about dataset construction and sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Define and justify the corpus size, time frame, and selection criteria for media/textual datasets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide details such as hours of radio analysed, number of episodes/articles, time range, and rationale. Example: Daykin et al. analysed 12 hours of radio to identify 703 comments about alcohol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and analyse stigma, framing, and stereotype perpetuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how media frames illness (e.g., as deviation from norms), perpetuates stigma, or moralises health behaviours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for discursive patterns that stigmatise (e.g., portrayals of mental illness as criminal/violent, or ageist framings of elderly health). Consider social consequences such as hindering help-seeking (Sontag, 1991).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple data sources for triangulation and richer interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine media sources (e.g., policy documents + interviews; news + social media in other chapter) to contextualise findings and triangulate interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including multiple naturally occurring sources can strengthen claims about representation, implementation, and audience effects. The chapter notes social media is covered elsewhere but recommends multi-source approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to institutional/organisational influences (financial and political) on content
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how media organisations' financial and political contexts shape reporting and representation choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that news selection and framing can be influenced by organisational imperatives; interpret content with awareness of these pressures (notable point: news is selective and influenced by financial and political circumstances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use predefined criteria and analytic tools where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When analysing structured documents (e.g., policy), use predefined criteria, coding schemes, or document maps to assess alignment and content systematically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cheung et al. used predefined criteria and document maps to measure alignment between policy determinants and intended outcomes; such structured tools aid replicability and comparability.
